title: Causal Effects of Single-Sex Schools on Long-Term Outcomes: Evidence from Random High School Assignment in South Korea
abstract: <jats:p>I explore the causal effects of single-sex high schools on long-term labor market outcomes using a unique feature of educational policy in South Korea—the random assignment of students into single-sex versus coeducational high schools. I find that the effect of single-sex schooling on earnings is positive for women but not for men. The effect is differential across job experience levels, increasing by 1.9 percentage points with each additional year of experience. Furthermore, women who graduated from single-sex schools are less likely to participate in the labor market than those who graduated from coeducational schools. Conversely, the effect of single-sex schooling on labor market participation is weakly positive for men. In addition, single-sex schooling affects other labor market outcomes, including women's work hours and job satisfaction. Finally, I use measurements of completed education and job training as human capital accumulation to study potential mechanisms through which single-sex schooling effects are asymmetric by gender.</jats:p>
